description:
Jodocus Hondius's map of Tartary, from the first Latin edition of the Mercator–Hondius Atlas (Amsterdam, 1606). It stretches from Muscovy and the Caspian to Korea and the strait of Anian, with two costume figures, an address to the reader, and notes on Gog and Magog, the tombs of the khans, Christian Tenduc, the Great Wall and asbestos.
An AI model, Claude Opus 5.5, read the map from the HKUST copy without any reference text: 99 texts and notes, which can be read in the panel and the tour, and 324 place names, shown under “Towns, rivers and lakes” in the filter.
Turn the sheet over for the atlas's description of Tartary (pp. 333–334), shown from the Utrecht University Library copy, in passages that follow its printed margin notes. The reading was compared with the project team's transcription, and every difference was checked on the scan by the AI, not yet by a person.

text.original:
In hac Tartariæ deſcriptione omnem adhibuimus diligentiam ut re:
giones nuper ab Anglis vel à Belgis alijſve detectæ ſuo quæq; loco habe:
rentur, quamvis mihi ipſi non ſatisfecerim, quis enim vaſtum illud et in:
cognitũ regnum verè deſcribet? at ut poßimus dum ut volumus non
licet. uſq; dum
melius quoddam
text.expanded: In hac Tartariæ descriptione omnem adhibuimus diligentiam ut regiones nuper ab Anglis vel à Belgis aliisve detectæ suo quæque loco haberentur, quamvis mihi ipsi non satisfecerim, quis enim vastum illud et incognitum regnum verè describet? at ut possimus dum ut volumus non licet. usque dum melius quoddam
text.translation: In this description of Tartary we have applied every diligence, so that the regions lately discovered by the English or by the Belgae [Netherlanders] or by others should each be held in its proper place, although I have not satisfied myself; for who will truly describe that vast and unknown kingdom? But [we do] as we can, since as we would is not allowed, until [there is] something better.
text.commentary:
The model's confidence in this reading: high.
Its note: Body of the address-to-the-reader cartouche (bottom left), six lines of italic. Lines 1-3 end in a colon used as a hyphen (re:|giones, habe:|rentur, in:|cognitũ). Line 4 ends 'non' followed by a long horizontal line-filler stroke; lines 5-6 are set narrow and centred in the semicircular lower lobe. 'alijſve' is engraved with ij; 'quæq;' and 'uſq;' use the q-with-3 (q;) abbreviation; 'cognitũ' has a macron/tilde over the u; 'poßimus' uses the ß ligature; accents on 'à' and 'verè'. The text ends 'melius quoddam' with no further words visible inside the frame; the sentence seems unfinished.
source: Read by Claude Opus 5.5 on 25 Nov 2026 from the HKUST copy, crops r5c1, r5c2, r6c1, r6c2, r6c3.

text.expanded: Tartaria, seu ut existimat Ioannes Leunclavius, Tataria, Regnum amplissimum est; præter enim Europæ partem, etiam Sarmatiam omnem Asiaticam complectitur, cum Scythia & Serica, quam nunc vocant Cathaio. Nomen habet a fluvio Tartaro, qui eam partem irrigat quæ a nostris Magog,
text.translation: Tartaria, or, as Ioannes Leunclavius [Johannes Löwenklau] thinks, Tataria, is a very large kingdom; for besides a part of Europe, it also takes in all Asiatic Sarmatia, together with Scythia and Serica, which they now call Cathaio. It has its name from the river Tartarus, which waters the part that is called Magog by our writers

text.expanded: ab accolis Mongul dicitur. Nam occidentalissimus eius Meridianus
text.translation: and Mongul by the inhabitants. It lies towards the north; on the east it has that most powerful kingdom of China; on the south India, the river Ganges and the Oxus; on the west the Caspian Sea and Poland; on that side it borders on Muscovy; and on the north on the Frozen Sea, where it is wholly unknown and is thought to be uninhabited and uncultivated. From the southern quarter to the north it occupies about xl [40] degrees, namely from the parallel of degree xl [40] of latitude to the parallel of degree xl [40]; and from east to west it extends more or less cxlv [145] degrees. text.translation: The rest I pass over, moving on to the buildings and public works. Here many remarkable things are met with, above all a very large and very beautiful palace, built of marble and adorned with gold, founded by the Cham Cublai [Kublai Khan] in the city of Ciandu. There is also another in the city of Cambalu, built with wonderful skill. Its circuit is about four miles, each side of the square comprising one mile. The wall is very thick, rising ten paces in height. Its outer surface shines with white and red colour. In each of the four corners of the wall a beautiful and large palace has been built to serve as a citadel. Likewise in the middle of each of the four walls an excellent palace has been built; and these are 8 in all. In these are kept arms, instruments, engines of war and machines: bows, arrows, quivers, spurs, bridles, lances, clubs, bowstrings, and the other things needed in war, and each kind of arms is placed in its own palace. Further, the face of the palace that looks to the south has 5 gates, of which the middle one, the largest of all, always remains shut and is never opened except for the King when he enters. Nor does anyone have entry through it except the King alone. But this face has two smaller gates at the side, through which the others who accompany the King enter. There are also three other gates, through which anyone may enter. Furthermore, within the wall already mentioned, another wall surrounds this royal castle, having in its corners and middle eight palaces, in which the King's other precious vessels are kept. In the inner middle space is the royal palace, namely the one in which the King lives. It has no upper storeys; but its pavement stands ten palms above the outer ground. The roof is very high and adorned with painting. The walls of the halls and chambers gleam with gold and silver. Everywhere very beautiful pictures and histories of warlike deeds present themselves to the eyes of those entering, glittering with vivid colours and shining gold. The larger hall comfortably admits up to 6 thousand people reclining at table. There are other things too, which, aiming at brevity, we omit. There is also beyond the river Pulisachniz a very beautiful marble bridge, whose length is three hundred paces and width 8, resting on twenty-four arches or vaults. There is also another in the city of Sindinfu, one mile long and eight paces wide.

text.translation: he must pay back ninefold. Those caught in adultery, man and woman alike, are put to death by the law itself. The Tartars are divided into hordes, a word which for them means a gathering and assembly of many. But as they inhabit various provinces lying far and wide apart, so neither do they all agree in customs or way of life. The men are square in build, with broad and fleshy faces, twisted and hollow eyes, rough only in the beard and shaven elsewhere; strong in body; bold in spirit; extremely tolerant of hunger and toil. When riding, if hunger and thirst have troubled them, they are accustomed to cut the veins of the horses they sit on and drink their blood. The nation is profane and barbarous: right for them lies in arms, law in strength and force. Many have no houses, but wagons instead. And since they roam with no fixed dwellings, they are accustomed to steer their course by the sight of the stars, especially of the Arctic Pole. They do not stay long in one place, thinking it a grave misfortune to remain long in the same place. They have no use for money, and so exchange goods for goods. They say they are Ishmaelites, and also openly profess it: they adopted the law of Mahomet in the year one thousand two hundred and forty-six. For the rest they keep the rite of the Jews: they are circumcised and they wash. Their supreme priest is the Seyd, their emperor the Cham. In some places very fine cloths are made, of gold and of silk, and also very clean linens. The Tartars feed on coarser foods, especially meats, and these raw or half-cooked; on milk and cheese. They abstain from pork. They drink mares' milk, which they know how to prepare so that it seems to be white wine, a drink not at all insipid. It is called by them Chuinis. They are most unclean in their way of life, inasmuch as they do not cover their tables with cloths, do not use napkins, since they wash neither their hands, nor their bodies, nor their clothes. They also drink water, milk, and beer brewed from millet. Wine for the most part does not grow among them; when it is imported, they drink it most greedily, like other men, to the point of drunkenness, which among them is a glory. As for trade, it flourishes greatly here in a number of cities, especially in gems, spices of every kind, and silk.
